svg.title: How to read a survival curve: where the median sits, and whose denominator each tail number belongs to
svg.desc: Schematic on how to read a glioblastoma survival curve. The main panel shows two survival curves over 0 to 5 years from randomisation, with the proportion still alive on the vertical axis. The upper curve is the radiotherapy plus temozolomide arm (n=287), with marked points at 27.2 per cent at two years (95 per cent confidence interval 22.2 to 32.5), 16.0 per cent at three years (12.0 to 20.6), 12.1 per cent at four years (8.5 to 16.4) and 9.8 per cent at five years (6.4 to 14.0). The lower curve is the radiotherapy alone arm (n=286): 10.9 per cent at two years, 4.4 per cent at three, 3.0 per cent at four and 1.9 per cent at five. A dashed vertical line at the median survival of 14.6 months is labelled, to its left, half of these people are to the left of this line, and to its right, half of them are to the right of it. At five years the curve has still not reached the floor, and the figure notes that the people on the tail are real. The curve shape is schematic; only the marked points are numbers reported in the paper. Below are three cards of equal size giving the denominator behind each tail number. First, the trial population: 9.8 per cent at five years (95 per cent confidence interval 6.4 to 14.0) from the radiotherapy plus temozolomide arm of EORTC 26981-22981 / NCIC CE.3, n=287, recruited 2000 to 2002, people who were randomised and whose age and performance status were good enough to enter a trial. Second, the real world: 4 per cent at five years (95 per cent confidence interval 2 to 5) from the Poon 2020 meta-analysis, 1,291 of 28,748 patients in cohorts recruited from 2005 onwards, where two- and three-year survival really did improve but five-year survival did not. Third, about 0.71 per cent at ten years from the Tykocki 2018 systematic review of 162 cases in 36 studies published 1950 to 2014, most without IDH testing, so that under the 2021 classification a substantial share would not be called glioblastoma today and the accurate sentence is that under the old classification some people lived ten years. A further panel gives a conditional probability: the probability of living another two years is 19.8 per cent at diagnosis and 65.9 per cent five years after diagnosis (Johnson 2012, SEER 1998 to 2008, patients whose treatment included radiotherapy, n=10,022), a population-level conditional probability and not anyone's personal forecast. At the foot of the figure is a warning: this curve is not a prediction for any one person, it is the statistics of a group; the median is not a deadline and the tail is not a promise; age, performance status, extent of resection and MGMT status push a person left or right, and the prognostic scoring tools explain only about a fifth of that variation, with the other four fifths unaccounted for.

g.text: HOW TO READ A SURVIVAL CURVE
Every number on the tail has its own
denominator
This figure asks you to see two things: what the median line actually
means, and that the tail is real.
The three tail numbers come from three different populations and
carry three different denominators — you cannot pick the highest one
and call it your expectation.
Survival curves from EORTC 26981-22981 / NCIC CE.3 (the curve shape is
schematic; only the marked points are numbers reported in the paper)

This curve is not a prediction for any one person
It is the statistics of a group. The median is not a deadline; the tail is not a
promise. For any one person, age, performance status, extent of resection
and MGMT status push them left or right — and the prognostic scoring tools
explain only about a fifth of that variation. The other four fifths we cannot
account for.
Schematic, redrawn from Stupp 2009 (EORTC 26981-22981 / NCIC CE.3), Poon
2020, Tykocki 2018 and Johnson 2012; the curve shape is schematic and only
the marked points are numbers reported in the papers; the cohorts, designs
and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be
compared directly.
